content: Kennel cough, also known as tracheobronchitis, is a highly contagious respiratory illness in dogs that involves inflammation of the upper respiratory tract. It can be caused by viral infections such as canine distemper, canine adenovirus, canine parainfluenza virus, or canine respiratory coronavirus, as well as bacterial infections like Bordetella bronchiseptica. The name kennel cough originates from the fact that the infection spreads rapidly among dogs in close quarters, such as in kennels. Both viral and bacterial causes of kennel cough are transmitted through airborne particles released when infected dogs sneeze or cough. The disease can also spread via contact with contaminated surfaces or through direct contact with infected dogs. It remains highly contagious even after symptoms have resolved, sometimes for days or weeks. Dogs are commonly exposed to the infection in environments where they are in close proximity to other dogs, such as pet stores, kennels, dog shows, and grooming facilities. Symptoms typically appear 3 to 5 days after exposure, and in some cases, the disease can progress to pneumonia. The clinical signs of kennel cough include a harsh, dry, hacking cough, retching, sneezing, snorting, or gagging. These symptoms may be triggered by light pressure on the trachea or by excitement and physical activity. Fever may or may not be present, depending on the individual case. The illness generally lasts between 10 to 20 days. Diagnosis is based on the observation of these symptoms and a history of exposure to other dogs. Treatment for kennel cough involves the use of antibiotics to address any bacterial infections that may be present. If the cough is non-productive (i.e., not bringing up any material), cough suppressants may be prescribed to provide relief. The prognosis for affected dogs is generally favorable. Prevention is achieved through vaccination against canine adenovirus, distemper, parainfluenza, and Bordetella bronchiseptica. In kennel environments, maintaining proper hygiene by disinfecting cages is crucial to preventing the spread of the disease. Most kennels require proof of vaccination before accepting dogs for boarding.
